tasks.short: Ask about symptoms before and at the visit, explain the repair, check with the user that it works, follow up later and note what was said.

steps.what: Customer answers the booking questions: error code, thermostat reading and a photo of the unit's display
Mechanic finds out the symptoms before the visit: by phone today; after the change by reading the booking answers and phoning only when they are unclear
Mechanic discusses the heating or cooling malfunctions with users on site to isolate problems
Mechanic explains the cause and the repair to the user
Mechanic checks with the user that the repairs corrected the malfunction
Mechanic checks the follow-up text for the job: customer, phone number and wording
Mechanic releases the follow-up text to be sent three days after the visit
Mechanic follows up days later to check the fix held: by phone to every customer today; after the change by phone only to customers who reply 'no'
Mechanic writes the user's account on the paper job sheet

tasks.design: The booking form in the firm's field service app ({OTHER}) asks the customer for the error code, what the thermostat shows and a photo of the unit's display, so the mechanic reads it before driving out. The mechanic checks and releases a follow-up text that goes three days after the visit to ask whether the system works; only 'no' replies get a call. Writing the user's account stays as it is. Talking with the user on site stays as it is.
tasks.previous_blocker: Symptoms were gathered by phone, and follow-ups were calls the mechanic often had no time for.
tasks.enabler_now: Field service apps for installers handle the job from request to invoice on the phone.
tasks.still_hard: Users describe symptoms loosely; photos of a home need care under privacy rules.
tasks.human_edge: Getting a worried customer to describe precisely when the noise starts.

ambition.what: Every repair followed up, not only when the mechanic finds time.

reach.learn: Whether structured booking questions cut call length.

evidence.claim: A field service app for installers runs digital work orders from quote to invoice with accounting links.
Photos of a customer's home are personal data to keep only for the job.

assumptions: Boundary: from the service request to the follow-up; the repair itself is outside.
Input contract: booking questions set by the service manager; answers and photos given by customers; fallback is the phone call.

Customer time is outside the mechanic's savings; answering the booking questions is step s0 (share 1). s1 keeps 60 for reading the answers and calling when they are unclear; s5 keeps 40 for calls after a 'no'. The user's account is a first record and keeps its full time; the text check and release keep theirs.
Conversations on site do not change.
unknowns: Share of customers who fill in the form.
research_questions: Do follow-up texts find failed repairs earlier?

incremental.description: No new upkeep: reading the booking answers is s1's remaining time.

approvals.approved_version: The follow-up text exactly as checked by the mechanic in s4c, sent once three days after the visit to the customer's number on the job; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most customers phone instead of using the form, so the pre-visit call stays (6.2); high: most customers answer the booking questions (10.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Agree visit times with customers, write work orders, requisition parts, order from stock, let the planner adjust, and confirm appointments.

steps.what: Customer picks a visit slot from the times the planning board offers
Mechanic phones customers to schedule work and agree visit times
Mechanic initiates work orders on paper with customer, address and unit details
Mechanic fills in house requisitions for parts from the warehouse
Office planner checks the schedule and moves jobs for emergencies
Mechanic prepares orders from stock or with the wholesaler: by phone today, from the work order after the change
Mechanic checks the final order: parts, quantities, supplier or warehouse and delivery point
Mechanic sends the checked order to the warehouse or wholesaler
Mechanic checks the next day's reminder texts: customers, addresses, dates and times
Mechanic confirms the next day's appointments: by ringing each customer today, by releasing the checked reminder texts after the change

tasks.design: Customers pick a slot from times offered by the planning board of the firm's field service app ({OTHER}), which proposes slots by rules on skills, region and job length; the mechanic handles exceptions. The booking creates the work order with the unit's history, requisitions and stock orders start from it and the mechanic checks each order before sending it, and checked reminder texts replace the confirmation call; the planner still reshuffles for emergencies.
tasks.previous_blocker: Scheduling and orders ran on phone calls and paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Field service apps run work orders from quote to invoice and offer booking slots.
tasks.still_hard: Emergencies upset the plan; some customers only phone.
tasks.human_edge: Fitting in an elderly customer without heating on a cold evening.
tasks.altitude: The mechanic handles exceptions instead of every booking; rescheduling stays with the planner.

evidence.claim: A field service app for installers runs digital work orders from quote to invoice with accounting links.
A fibre network firm with 500 technicians reports about 8 hours per technician per week saved on work-order mail, entry and reports (vendor case, period not stated).
Rule-based scheduling on skills and region is outside the high-risk AI category.

assumptions: Boundary: from the service request to the confirmed appointment and ordered parts; the visit is outside.
Input contract: skills, regions and job lengths kept by the service planner; unit history from past work orders; stock levels kept by the warehouse clerk; fallback is the phone.
Planner and warehouse time is outside the mechanic's savings.

Emergency reshuffling does not change. The customer's slot choice is step s0 (share 1). s1 keeps 50 for customers who phone and for exceptions; s2 keeps 40 for work orders from phone bookings; s3 keeps 50; s5 keeps 60 for building the order; s6 keeps 20 for releasing the texts; both checks and the send keep their full time.
research_questions: Do reminder texts reduce no-access visits?

already_counted.description: Mechanic reviews bookings that break the rules.

incremental.description: Service planner keeps job lengths and regions current.
No ongoing upkeep for the mechanic: learning the planning and order screens is a one-off.

approvals.approved_version: The order with parts, quantities and delivery point exactly as checked by the mechanic in s5c, sent once to the warehouse or the named wholesaler; any change needs a new check.
The next day's reminder texts with customer, address, date and time exactly as checked by the mechanic in s6c, sent once to the customers' numbers on the work orders; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most customers phone instead of booking, so scheduling and work orders stay largely by hand (31.7); high: most customers book a slot (52.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Estimate materials for the job, order them, pick them up or have them delivered, install them and book what was used.

steps.what: Mechanic estimates the materials and supplies needed for the job
Mechanic prepares the materials order: by phone to the wholesaler today, from the work order after the change
Mechanic checks the final materials order: items, quantities, delivery day and van or pick-up point
Mechanic sends the checked order to the wholesaler's ordering link
Mechanic drives to the wholesaler to pick up materials
Mechanic delivers and installs materials to maintain equipment in good working condition
Mechanic books the materials actually used for invoicing: from receipts and lists today, on the work order starting from the ordered list after the change

tasks.design: Standard materials lists per job type in the firm's field service app ({OTHER}) give a first estimate that the mechanic adjusts, and the mechanic checks the order and sends it once from the work order to the wholesaler's ordering link. Orders placed the day before are delivered to the van or a pick-up point; the mechanic books the materials actually used on the work order for the invoice, and installing stays manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Each job's materials were worked out, phoned in and fetched by the mechanic.
tasks.enabler_now: Field service apps run work orders from quote to invoice; wholesalers take electronic orders and deliver.
tasks.still_hard: Repairs reveal surprises; a missing part still means a trip.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which fitting this old installation will really need.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; fewer trips and calls.

reach.learn: Whether standard lists let the warehouse pre-pack.

evidence.claim: A field service app for installers runs digital work orders from quote to invoice with accounting links.
Installation wholesalers take electronic orders and deliver to vans or pick-up points.

assumptions: Boundary: from the materials estimate to materials booked; invoicing is outside.
Input contract: standard materials lists per job type kept by the service manager; wholesaler catalogue and ordering link from the wholesaler; fallback is phone and pick-up.
Wholesaler time is outside the mechanic's savings.

Installing, the order check and the send keep their full time. s1 keeps 60 for adjusting the standard list; s2 keeps 40 for building the order; s3 keeps 60 for pick-ups that remain; s5 keeps 30 for booking actual use.
unknowns: Whether the wholesaler delivers to vans in the region.
Share of jobs with standard materials.
research_questions: How many wholesaler trips per week disappear?

already_counted.description: Mechanic adjusts the standard materials list.

incremental.description: Mechanic orders a day ahead instead of on the day.

approvals.approved_version: The materials order with items, quantities and delivery point exactly as checked by the mechanic in s2c, sent once to the wholesaler's ordering link; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly repair work with unknown parts, so standard lists fit poorly and trips to the wholesaler stay (17.5); high: mostly planned jobs ordered a day ahead (28.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check risks before work, follow safety procedures for refrigerants, gas and power, keep the F-gas logbook, clean the work area and keep certificates current.

steps.what: Mechanic does a last-minute risk check before starting: on paper today, as a checklist in the work order after the change
Mechanic follows safety procedures for refrigerants, gas and electricity
Mechanic writes leak checks and refrigerant added or recovered in the paper logbook
Mechanic keeps the work area clean and removes waste
Mechanic tracks refrigerant and gas certificate expiry dates on paper

tasks.design: The risk check is a short checklist in the mobile work order of the field service app ({OTHER}), and the refrigerant logbook fields (leak check, refrigerant type, amount added and recovered) sit in the same work order, so unit and refrigerant data fill from past work orders and the mechanic writes the amounts. Certificate expiry dates sit in the {LMS} with reminders; safe work and cleaning stay with the mechanic.
tasks.previous_blocker: Risk checks and refrigerant logbooks were paper kept at the unit or in the van.
tasks.enabler_now: Mobile work orders can carry checklists and logbook fields.
tasks.still_hard: Logbook entries must be right; a ticked checklist is not safe work.
tasks.human_edge: Stopping when a gas smell or a live wire is not where it should be.

reach.task: Keep refrigerant records for owned units
reach.learn: Whether owners get complete logbooks from the work orders.

evidence.claim: The EU F-gas Regulation sets leak checks and logbook rules for HVAC records; logbook fields can sit in the work order.
A maintenance app drafts checklists for review and prompts to confirm unusual readings.
Work orders with time stamps or location can observe technicians and need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the risk check to a clean work area; incident reporting is outside.
Input contract: checklist items and logbook fields set by the service manager; unit data from past work orders; certificate dates entered by the office; fallback is paper.
Checklists are not used to judge mechanics.

Safe work, cleaning and the risk check keep their full time. s3 keeps 80 because only unit and refrigerant details fill in and the leak check and amounts are still written; s5 keeps 50 because reminders replace tracking dates on paper.
unknowns: Share of jobs with refrigerant work.
research_questions: Are digital refrigerant logbooks more complete at inspections?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: learning the checklist and logbook screens is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few units have past work orders in the app, so logbook details are still written in full (5.0); high: unit data on file (8.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The HVAC mechanic keeps diagnosis, safe work and customer contact; scheduling, ordering and paper logbooks shrink.
skills_to_grow: Working from a mobile work order
role.ambitious_version: A mechanic who arrives knowing the problem, with the parts in the van, and leaves with the record done.
